messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Park Ranger
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 40

**Case Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 41-year-old South Asian man who presents for therapy at the urging of his partner, Maya. He is a park ranger for a large national forest, a job he has held for the past twelve years. He describes himself as having always been a quiet, observant person who found peace in the solitude of the backcountry. He speaks slowly, choosing his words with care, and often looks down at his hands as he talks.

The trauma occurred three years ago, during a routine solo patrol in a remote section of the park. He was checking a trail for storm damage when he came upon a group of men illegally harvesting timber. They were armed. Before he could radio for backup, he was surrounded, disarmed, and forced into the back of their truck. For the next 72 hours, he was held in a small, abandoned hunting cabin. He was bound, blindfolded, and kept in a state of near-total sensory deprivation. He had no idea where he was or if anyone was looking for him. He was given water but very little food. The men spoke to him only to threaten him, telling him that if he made a sound, they would leave him in the woods for the animals. He describes the experience not as a series of violent acts, but as a profound, crushing silence punctuated by the sound of his own heartbeat and the rough feel of the rope on his wrists.

He was eventually rescued when a search party, using a helicopter, spotted the truck. The men were arrested. Mr. A. was physically unharmed, but he says he “hasn’t felt right” since that day.

In the months following the rescue, he returned to work. He felt he had to. The park was his life. But he found he could no longer tolerate the quiet. The silence of the forest, once a source of comfort, now feels like a threat. He finds himself constantly scanning the tree line, listening for footsteps that aren’t there. His heart races when a branch snaps. He has started taking a partner on every patrol, a practice he once resisted as an intrusion on his solitude. He now carries a satellite phone that he checks obsessively, and he has memorized the coordinates of every ranger station. He feels a deep, unshakable shame about this, believing he has become weak.

His sleep is fragmented. He has recurrent nightmares, not of the men or the threats, but of the sensory details: the feeling of the blindfold pressing against his eyes, the smell of damp earth and stale cigarette smoke, the cold metal of the handcuffs. He wakes up with his hands clenched, his body rigid. He avoids the section of the park where it happened, claiming it is “just easier” to let other rangers handle that area. When Maya asks him about his day, he gives one-word answers. He has withdrawn from their shared activities, like hiking and cooking, preferring to sit alone on the back porch, staring at the yard.

He arrived at the session today after a particularly difficult week. He had been assigned to lead a group of schoolchildren on a nature walk. He found himself unable to speak. For a full minute, he stood in front of the children, his mind blank, a feeling of pressure building in his chest. He eventually excused himself, leaving the group with a volunteer. He told his supervisor it was a panic attack. He tells me he feels like he is “living inside a glass box,” watching the world from a distance but unable to touch it. He says he is tired. He is tired of being vigilant, tired of the shame, and tired of the constant, low-grade dread that has replaced the stillness he once loved.
